item.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계 at Lathrop Library
item.description:
The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future. The exhibition explores Kim’s concept of “Indigenous Futures” through art as a form of civilizational transformation, expressing p'owŏl (포월 抱越), embracing and transcending the pain and contradictions of reality while reaching toward new possibilities for the future.

The opening reception on October 8 will feature an artist talk and a Korean mask dance (탈춤 t'alch'um) performance by Kim Bong-Jun and Che Se-hyun, a Seattle-based creative director and multidisciplinary artist.

The exhibition is curated by Jee-Young Park, Korean Studies Librarian, and Jisoo Kim, an SFSU MA Museum Studies graduate and San Francisco-based curator.

item.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026) at Green Library, Bing Wing
item.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day. The exhibition includes microscope images revealing the textile structure of the woven text as well as a woven enlargement that illustrates its basic principles, along with several artworks inspired by or related to the themes of the exhibition.

item.title: Electric Contrasts: the Art of the Detail at McMurtry Building
item.description:
Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail brings together photobooks and magazines to show how the revolution of photography in the late 19th and early 20th century changed the history of art. Electric Contrasts takes Kenneth Clark’s landmark 1938 book One Hundred Details from Pictures in the National Gallery as a starting point to illuminate the impact black and white photographic details of Old Master paintings had on new ways of seeing in the early 20th century. The exhibition reveals the anachronistic and provocative juxtapositions of artworks in avant-garde magazines and books which created a radically new vision that would go on to influence television and the internet.

Curated by Altair Brandon-Salmon. Bowes Art & Architecture Library hours: M-Th 9-7pm; Friday 9-5pm; Sunday 12-6pm.

Tour by Dr. Brandon-Salmon on 9/5 at 6 pm prior to Electric Contrasts Study Evening.

item.title: A Vision of Paris: The Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford at Green Library, Bing Wing
item.description:
Stanford University Libraries presents A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford, on view in the Peterson Gallery and Munger Rotunda of the Cecil H. Green Library from September 22, 2026 to January 24, 2027. 

Roxane Debuisson (1927–2018) dedicated sixty years to documenting the transformation of the city of Paris during the nineteenth century.  If Roxane Debuisson could not stop the changes she saw underway in the late 20th century, she could at least preserve the city’s earlier history through images, literature, guidebooks, and other documents. 

Her lifelong project helped to document Paris during the nineteenth century, especially the city’s rapid changes from the 1850s to the 1870s, when Emperor Napoleon III and his prefect of the Seine, Baron Eugène Haussmann, transformed the city with new boulevards, green spaces, and public utilities, and fostered innovations in commercial and cultural practices. 

A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford draws upon the extensive array of commercial almanacs, prints, postcards, commercial ephemera, stereographs, manuscripts, historic photographs, and other items that are a part of the Roxane Debuisson Collection of Paris history, circa 1789-1970, acquired by the Department of Special Collections at Stanford University Libraries in 2020. These materials place Paris as the birthplace of political, commercial, and urban innovations, and as a city defined by the tension between its historical past and its continuous reinvention. The exhibit highlights the city’s rapid changes and their diverse causes, while suggesting the collection’s vast possibilities for both research and instruction.

This exhibition is curated by Sarah Sussman, Assistant University Librarian for Collections and Services & Curator of French and Italian Collections, Stanford University Libraries, and Chloe Summers Edmondson, Assistant Professor of French at the University of Miami. Produced and designed by Deardra Fuzzell, with assistance from Kylee Jo Diedrich, Sofia McGullam Ornelas, and Pasha Tope.

A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford will be open to the public. Registration at the entrance with a valid government ID is required to enter the Cecil H. Green Library and view the exhibit.

item.title: Emergent Properties: Decennial Reflections on Collections at David Rumsey Map Center (Green Library)
item.description:
In 2026 the David Rumsey Map Center celebrates its tenth year—a moment to reflect on how the Center has added value to scholarship on campus and around the world. Our collections are vast and not bounded by geography, spanning the 15th century to the present. Yet over the last decade, certain materials have repeatedly resonated with the students, instructors, and researchers who frequent the Center. Emergent Properties brings together a selection of highlights from deep within the collections of the David Rumsey Map Center: items that have not only proven to be rare or beautiful, but have become the drivers of scholarship, programming, and support areas that have resonated with our users. The forty objects in this exhibition represent these emergent properties. Though only a glimpse into the full breadth of the Center’s holdings, they reflect what has mattered most over the past ten years. 

Join us for an exhibition reception on Friday, November 20 at 3pm. The reception will feature a tour of the exhibition by David Rumsey Map Center staff. Please register to attend.

The exhibition will be on display at the David Rumsey Map Center within Green Library through Friday, March 5, 2027.

item.title: Estonia at the Front Line: Security, Resilience, and Technology: A Discussion with the Prime Minister of Estonia Kristen Michal at Encina Hall
item.description:
Join us for an engaging discussion with Prime Minister of the Republic of Estonia Kristen Michal on:

Estonia at the Front Line: Security, Resilience, and Technology: Security, Europe, and Technology

Estonia sits at the intersection of some of the defining challenges of our time. Bordering Russia and on NATO’s eastern flank, Estonia has had to make security and resilience a national priority. At the same time, it has emerged as one of the world’s most digitally advanced societies. For Estonia, security, agility and innovation are not abstract ideas -- they are necessities.

In this conversation with Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal, we will explore what it means to lead a country on NATO’s eastern flank at a time of profound geopolitical change; why the outcome of Russia’s war against Ukraine will shape Europe and the wider world; and how Europe can take greater responsibility for its own security.

We will also discuss Estonia’s remarkable evolution into one of the world’s most advanced digital societies, its ambitions in artificial intelligence, and what smaller countries can teach us about adapting when new technologies are reshaping economies, governments and societies.


The discussion will be moderated by Michael McFaul, Ken Olivier and Angela Nomellini Professor of International Studies, Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution, at the Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies and at the Woods Institute for the Environment.

Kristen Michal has served as Prime Minister of Estonia since July 2024. He leads one of the world’s most digital countries, with a strong focus on the next wave of innovation: AI. His government aims to make Estonia one of the world’s top 10 innovation leaders, accelerate the use of AI across the economy and public sector, and create an environment where new technologies and companies can grow and scale. Estonia has spent decades building a digital state where almost all public services are available online. Today, the country is focused on bringing the same ambition to AI, from education and public services to business, science and defence. Prime Minister Michal has made innovation, competitiveness and the smarter use of technology central to Estonia’s economic agenda. Security is another defining priority. Estonia is investing more than 5% of GDP in defence and has a rapidly growing defence technology sector. It is also one of Ukraine’s strongest supporters and advocates for a stronger European role in security and defence.

Before becoming Prime Minister, Michal served as Minister of Climate, Minister of Economic Affairs and Infrastructure, and Minister of Justice. As a member of parliament, he chaired the Economic Affairs Committee, working on telecommunications, e-services, cybersecurity and new transport solutions. He is also a reserve officer in the Estonian Defence Forces.

Opening remarks will be delivered by University Librarian Michael Keller.

The in-person event is free and open to the public. RSVP is requested.

This event is part of Global Conversations, a series of talks, lectures, and seminars hosted by Stanford University Libraries and Vabamu with the goal of educating scholars, students, leaders, and the public on the benefits of but also challenges related to sustaining freedom.

item.title: Two Views of the Chinese Coast at David Rumsey Map Center (Green Library)
item.description:
Join us for "Two Views of the Chinese Coast," a talk by Kären Wigen, the Frances & Charles Field Professor in Stanford's Department of History, at the David Rumsey Map Center. When cartographic collections began to appear online in the 1990s, historians of East Asia were quick to seize on maps as subjects for research. Over the next thirty years, a sophisticated field of critical map studies developed, illuminating the lively landscape of cartographic production across the early modern Sinosphere. While map-focused research made rapid strides, a gap gradually opened between cartographic research (the history of maps) and what we might call map-informed history (history with maps). 

This talk attempts to address that gap by investigating two works from Stanford University Libraries’ collections: a Qing-era scroll painting of the Pacific coast, housed in the David Rumsey Map Collection, and a British map of the same shoreline from 1859, owned by a private collector and held digitally within the Barry Lawrence Ruderman Map Collection. During the 19th century, both maps served as tools of military planning; where the Qing scroll was likely consulted for coastal defense, the British chart was designed for a naval attack. By putting them in dialogue with each other, the talk suggests how cross-cultural map comparison can help us tell more complex, entangled stories about Euro-Asian interaction.

Speaker Bio

Kären Wigen teaches Japanese history and the history of cartography. A geographer by training, she earned her doctorate at the University of California at Berkeley. Her first book, The Making of a Japanese Periphery, 1750-1920 (1995), mapped the economic transformation of southern Nagano Prefecture during the heyday of the silk industry. Her second book, A Malleable Map: Geographies of Restoration in Central Japan, 1600-1912 (2010), returned to the ground of that study, exploring the roles of cartography, chorography, and regionalism in the making of modern Shinano.  An abiding interest in world history led her to co-author The Myth of Continents (1997) with Martin Lewis. She also introduced a forum on oceans in history for the American Historical Review and co-edited Seascapes: Maritime Histories, Littoral Cultures, and Transoceanic Exchanges (2007) with Jerry Bentley and Renate Bridenthal. Her latest book is Territorial Imaginaries: Beyond the Sovereign Map (2025).

item.title: OpenADMET - Raising the bar on ADMET prediction with open science (Bay Area Open Science Group Meeting)
item.description:
This month, Dr. Pat Walters is joining us to talk about the OpenADMET initiative. Drug discovery programs frequently stall due to the Avoid-ome, which comprises the complex off-target interactions and ADMET liabilities that traditional heuristic methods struggle to address. To solve this, OpenADMET combines high-resolution structural biology, directed data generation, and machine learning into a systematic framework for predicting and mitigating these liabilities. Central to this mission is generating targeted datasets to host large-scale blind benchmarks that test community predictive models on real-world drug design problems. By uniting hundreds of academic and industry teams through these challenges, webinars, and conferences, the initiative fosters widespread collaboration to establish transparent, data-driven standards across the field.

About the Bay Area Open Science Group
The Bay Area Open Science Group is a growing community for Bay Area academics and researchers interested in incorporating open science into their research, teaching, and learning. Targeting students, faculty, and staff at UCSF, Berkeley, and Stanford, the goal of the community is to increase awareness of and engagement with all things open science, including open access articles, open research data, open source software, and open educational resources. Through this work the group hopes to connect researchers with tools they can use to make the products and process of science more equitable and reproducible.

item.title: Book Event with Roland Betancourt and T.L. Taylor, "Disneyland and the Rise of Automation" at Green Library, Bing Wing
item.description:
Please join the Silicon Valley Archives in welcoming Roland Betancourt and T.L. Taylor as they discuss Betancourt's latest book, Disneyland and Rise of Automation, on December 2, 2026, at 4:30 p.m. 

 

Disneyland and the Rise of Automation argues that theme park rides are factory assembly lines in disguise, ones that manufacture subjects rather than products. The book traces the technological systems that made this possible, from limit switches and relay racks to programmable logic controllers and magnetic tape, revealing how innovations developed for wartime manufacturing and Cold War industry found new life in the Happiest Place on Earth. It applies insights from the history of technology to problems shared by historians, media scholars, and critics of visual culture, such as the aesthetics of automation and the politics of labor.

  

Roland Betancourt is a Chancellor’s Professor at the University of California, Irvine. He is currently the Andrew W. Mellon Professor at the Center for Advanced Study in the Visual Arts at the National Gallery of Art. A 2023 Guggenheim Fellow, he has published books on Byzantine visual culture, gender, and sexuality, including the prize-winning Byzantine Intersectionality (Princeton, 2020).

 

T.L. Taylor is Professor of Comparative Media Studies at MITand affiliate faculty member in Anthropology and Women’s and Gender Studies. She is a qualitative sociologist who has focused on the interrelations between culture and technology in online environments for over thirty years. Her work sits at the intersection of sociology, media studies, and science and technology studies.

item.title: Film Screening of the Latvian submission for the Academy Awards – Ulya at Bishop Auditorium
item.description:
Join us for a film screening of Latvia's submission for the Academy Awards and commentary from Dr. Karla Oeler, Director of the Center for Russian, Eastern European, and Eurasian Studies and Associate Professor of Film and Media Studies in the Department of Art & Art History.

Ulya (2026) is a true story about Uljana Semjonova, who is a very tall girl living on a remote farm in Soviet Latvia in 1964. Her height, almost two meters, worries her family, who aren't sure how she will fit into the world. When her class photo reaches basketball coaches, she is taken to Riga to train with TTT Riga. She works hard but feels torn, because basketball doesn't give her the ordinary life she dreams of. After running away back home, she realizes that both the village and the sport see her only as "the tall girl." When she finally accepts herself, she must decide whether to stay hidden or try to become the best basketball player in the world.

Dr. Karla Oeler is the Director of the Center for Russian, Eastern European, and Eurasian Studies and an Associate Professor of Film and Media Studies in the Department of Art & Art History. Her research and teaching interests are film history, theory and criticism, with emphases including the theory and practice of Sergei Eisenstein, cinematic representations of violence and thinking, and the relations between film aesthetics, literature, theory and philosophy. She is the author of A Grammar of Murder:  Violent Scenes and Film Form (University of Chicago Press, 2009).  Her work has appeared in numerous forums including Cinema Journal, The Journal of Visual Culture, and Slavic Review on a range of topics including works by Fyodor Dostoevsky, Jean-Luc Godard, Sergei Parajanov, and Jean Renoir.  She is currently writing a book called “The Surface of Things:  Cinema and Interiority.”  

This event is free and open to the public. Registration is required.
